cards.back: A value — and some also change an operand (a side effect)
cards.extra: Assignment returns the assigned value, which is why a = b = c works. Operators that only produce values leave their operands alone.

cards.front: You are unsure of operator precedence. What should you do?
cards.back: Add parentheses — say what you mean rather than testing what the compiler does
cards.extra: The book's two near-identical expressions give different results purely from grouping. Multiplication before addition is the only rule most people reliably remember.

cards.front: When you assign one object variable to another, what is copied?
cards.back: The reference — both variables now name the same object
cards.extra: The book calls this aliasing: modifying through either name changes the single object. There is no automatic copy of the object.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::20 Pass by Value vs Pass by Reference

cards.front: What does == compare on two objects?
cards.back: The references — whether they point at the same object
cards.extra: It never looks at contents. Two separately built Strings holding "x" are not ==; the book's title for this is "testing object equivalence".
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::20 Pass by Value vs Pass by Reference

cards.front: What does equals() do by default, and what must you do to change that?
cards.back: By default it is identity; override it to compare contents
cards.extra: Object.equals behaves like ==. Classes such as String override it, which is why "a".equals(x) tests characters while == tests identity.
cards.merge_into: 00 Java Roadmap::02 Object Model::20 Pass by Value vs Pass by Reference

cards.front: What does && guarantee that & does not?
cards.back: The right operand is not evaluated when the left is false
cards.extra: Short-circuiting is what makes null guards work: s != null && s.length() > 0. With & both sides always run.

cards.front: Integer division: what is 7 / 2 and how do you get 3.5?
cards.extra: Both operands int means int arithmetic, truncated toward zero. This is the single most common surprise in numeric code.

cards.front: What does a narrowing cast such as (int) 3.9 do?
cards.back: Truncates toward zero — it does not round
cards.extra: 3.9 becomes 3, and −3.9 becomes −3. Rounding needs Math.round, which returns a long.

cards.front: Which types are promoted to int before arithmetic?
cards.extra: So byte b = 1; b = b + 1; fails — the addition produces an int. This promotion is why small integer arithmetic never overflows in place.

cards.back: >> fills with the sign bit; >>> fills with zeros
cards.extra: For negative numbers they diverge sharply: −8 >> 1 is −4, while −8 >>> 1 is a large positive int.
